text: The Bloch sphere from the last lesson has a hard limit: it only describes one qubit at a time, and it breaks down entirely for entangled states. The Q-sphere and state-city plots exist precisely to cover that gap.

The Q-sphere places every computational basis state at a fixed position on a sphere. Each basis state with nonzero probability in your statevector appears as a blob: size encodes probability, color encodes relative phase. State-city takes a different approach to the same data — a 3D bar chart with one pair of bars per basis state, real and imaginary amplitude components, showing the raw structure a Bloch sphere can't represent for an entangled system.
Here's real output from Qiskit's own documentation showing exactly that: basis states with nonzero probability rendered as blobs, nothing drawn anywhere else.

Take the familiar Bell state. Feed its statevector into plot_state_qsphere and you get exactly two blobs, at the 00 and 11 positions, nothing anywhere else. Both blobs are the same size, because both basis states carry equal 0.5 probability. Both are the same color, because both amplitudes are the same positive real number — no relative phase difference. That's the direct visual signature of the Bell state's entanglement.

Extend to three qubits with the GHZ state, amplitudes on 000 and 111 only. The Q-sphere scales up without changing the underlying logic: two equal-size, equal-color blobs, nothing at the other six positions. Nothing conceptually new happened going from two qubits to three — the Q-sphere simply has more basis-state positions available, which is exactly why it scales cleanly where a single 3D arrow built for one qubit cannot.
Chapter 4 closes with a lab that puts histogram, Bloch sphere, and Q-sphere side by side, and builds the judgment to pick the right one for the right audience.
